title: Normalized Determinants and Height Metrics
subtitle: Quillen isometry, Deligne pairing, and good reduction
summary: An exact normalized projection-formula isometry and its rank-zero, curve-correspondence, and good-reduction consequences, with full proofs.
evidence: The full supplied determinant comparison arguments are retained. Bad-reduction and general family comparisons remain separate research questions.
html:
1. Introduction

The comparison between a cycle-theoretic height and a determinant construction has two parts. One must identify the underlying line, and one must identify its metric with the correct normalization. The second part contains a genuine constant ambiguity even when the two curvature forms agree. A Jacobian family provides a useful setting in which that ambiguity can be removed exactly.

Let CCC be a pointed smooth projective complex curve and J=Pic⁡0(C)J=\operatorname{Pic}^0(C)J=Pic0(C). The standard Poincaré metric on C×JC\times JC×J has purely mixed curvature. In a determinant family obtained by twisting a fixed complex with the Poincaré bundle, the family index formula therefore depends only on the virtual rank of its pushforward to CCC. Dividing by the determinant fibre at the origin equips the line with a unit rigidification. Equality of curvature forms then gives equality of metrics: their logarithmic ratio is pluriharmonic on the compact connected variety JJJ, and its value at the origin is zero.

This argument proves the projection-formula isometry in Theorem 2.1. Its rank-zero specialization is Theorem 2.2. Applied to a curve correspondence, the two theorems give Corollary 2.3; the relevant rank and determinant are computed by the leading terms of Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch. The good-reduction analogue is Proposition 2.4. There the quotient of two model lines has a vertical divisor, and the unit rigidification forces its coefficient to vanish.

The full arguments appear in the next section in this order. Throughout, CH⁡j(X)Q\operatorname{CH}^j(X)_{\mathbf Q}CHj(X)Q​ denotes the rational Chow group, and Vj(X)=ker⁡(CH⁡j(X)Q⟶H2j(X,Q))V^j(X)=\ker\bigl(\operatorname{CH}^j(X)_{\mathbf Q}\longrightarrow H^{2j}(X,\mathbf Q)\bigr)Vj(X)=ker(CHj(X)Q​⟶H2j(X,Q)) over C\mathbf CC. The cochain determinant convention and the Poincaré normalization are fixed explicitly before the comparison theorems. The determinant–biextension identifications of [3; 4] explain how this comparison enters local height formulas.

2. Normalized determinants on Jacobian families

2.1. The Poincaré metric and normalization

Its Chern form Ω=c1(P)\Omega=c_1(\mathcal P)Ω=c1​(P) is purely mixed: it has real degree one in CCC and degree one in JJJ.

Choose fixed Kähler metrics on the varieties involved.

The determinant lines with their Quillen metrics are smooth on the whole JJJ, including cohomology-jump loci. Under the algebraic isomorphism, the logarithm of the ratio of their metrics is therefore a smooth pluriharmonic function on the compact connected manifold JJJ. It is constant, and the norm-one origin rigidifications make that constant zero. Changing the hermitian representatives or the fixed product metrics preserves both the curvature computation and this normalization, proving the last assertion. ◻

Changing the chosen cycle lifts by higher filtration changes their product only in codimension at least n+2n+2n+2, which is zero on C×XC\times XC×X; the rational Chern character then gives the same normalized line. ◻

The relation to the classical archimedean height uses the determinant–cycle–Hodge biextension comparison of [3, Propositions 4.3, 4.29, 4.31 and Corollary 4.32]. Its disjoint-cycle trivialization gives the local height [3, Remark 4.7]. The relative comparison over a smooth base is given in [4, Theorem 10.9]; that theorem includes an inversion of the central Gm\mathbf G_mGm​ under its conventions. Fixing the cochain determinant convention above and the corresponding Poincaré convention fixes this sign.

An incidence locus can be a zero or pole locus of the chosen meromorphic frame without being a singularity of the line metric. The second term is smooth across incidence in the Jacobian family just constructed. This global line comparison resolves the normalization and continuity issue for that determinant model.

2.5. The source-curve good-reduction comparison

Let O\mathcal OO be a complete discrete valuation ring with fraction field KvK_vKv​, equipped with a fixed non-Archimedean absolute value inducing the given discrete valuation. Let C/O\mathcal C/\mathcal OC/O be a smooth proper geometrically connected curve with a section, let J/O\mathcal J/\mathcal OJ/O be its Jacobian, and let P\mathcal PP be the axis-rigidified Poincaré bundle. For a perfect complex KKK on C\mathcal CC, form the normalized determinant line DC(K)\mathcal D_{\mathcal C}(K)DC​(K) on J\mathcal JJ by the same algebraic construction.

Proposition 2.4. Suppose the generic virtual rank of KKK is zero and deg⁡det⁡KKv=0\deg\det K_{K_v}=0degdetKKv​​=0. The model metric of DC(K)\mathcal D_{\mathcal C}(K)DC​(K) on the generic fibre is the canonical rigidified Poincaré metric associated with det⁡KKv\det K_{K_v}detKKv​​.

Proof. The degree of det⁡K\det KdetK is zero on every fibre. After rigidification along the section, it defines a point of the relative Pic⁡0\operatorname{Pic}^0Pic0, and hence a rigidified Poincaré extension on J\mathcal JJ. The rank-zero determinant identity on the generic curve identifies its generic line with DC(K)\mathcal D_{\mathcal C}(K)DC​(K), respecting the origin rigidification.

Regard this isomorphism as a rational section of the quotient of the two model lines. Its divisor is vertical. The abelian scheme J\mathcal JJ is regular and its special fibre is geometrically integral, so this divisor is a[Js]a[\mathcal J_s]a[Js​] for an integer aaa. Pullback to the zero section has valuation aaa, but the two integral unit rigidifications make that valuation zero. Thus a=0a=0a=0. Normality extends the isomorphism and its inverse over the whole model. The model metrics coincide. The Poincaré multiplication laws extend over the abelian scheme and are isometries, identifying this model metric with the canonical one. ◻

If an ambient model X\mathcal XX and a model-perfect complex on C×X\mathcal C\times\mathcal XC×X have a perfect derived pushforward to C\mathcal CC, the determinant projection formula reduces their model comparison to this proposition. At a bad-reduction source curve the vertical correction involves the geometry of a semistable or Néron model; this is a separate comparison problem.

3. The remaining metric comparisons

The comparisons above provide the complex-place and good-reduction inputs for a local height comparison. The next step is to identify the vertical correction at a place of semistable reduction.

Problem 3.1 (Semistable source curves). Fix a complete discretely valued field KvK_vKv​ with its original absolute value, a pointed smooth projective geometrically connected curve C/KvC/K_vC/Kv​, and a semistable model C\mathcal CC. Let KKK be a perfect complex on the model with generic virtual rank zero and deg⁡det⁡KKv=0\deg\det K_{K_v}=0degdetKKv​​=0. Construct the admissible correction to its normalized determinant model metric and identify the resulting rigidified metric with the canonical Poincaré metric attached to det⁡KKv\det K_{K_v}detKKv​​. For a determinant arising from a curve correspondence, compare this metric with the actual-form Green construction, retaining the finite local lengths, prescribed cycle representatives and native finite-extension degree.

In the smooth-model case, Proposition 2.4 supplies this comparison. At semistable reduction the correction must account for the components and intersection graph. Passage to an actual-form height also uses its trace, correspondence covariance and normalization on the complete actual test space.

The corresponding family problem concerns both the boundary and the growth of the resulting height. One can formulate a precise target without asserting that every family has positive height growth.

Let FFF be a number field, S/FS/FS/F a smooth quasi-projective variety, and f:X→Sf:\mathcal X\to Sf:X→S a smooth projective family of relative dimension 2r−12r-12r−1. Such an inequality would give finiteness of bounded-height points of bounded degree on UUU by the classical Northcott theorem for hAh_AhA​. It is a statement about the parameter space, distinct from Northcott for all integral classes in one fixed Chow group. The relative biextension comparison over a smooth base is [4, Theorem 10.9]. Its singular-fibre extension in Theorem 11.2 requires a modified cycle with a specified cohomological property; Lemma 11.1 obtains that modification under the Hodge conjecture. These conditions belong to the boundary comparison in Problem 3.2.

abstractHtml: We compare normalized determinant-of-cohomology metrics on Jacobian families. For a perfect complex on the product of a pointed curve and a smooth projective variety, the derived projection formula, for product Kähler metrics, induces an exact isometry after normalization at the origin. In virtual rank zero, the resulting line is the Deligne pairing with the determinant of the pushforward. Filtered Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch identifies the line attached to a curve correspondence and a homologically trivial cycle. At a finite place where the pointed source curve has good reduction, a model-perfect complex of generic virtual rank zero and degree-zero determinant yields the canonical rigidified Poincaré model metric.
